title: Instagram Edits: a cleaner path from clip to post
excerpt: Use Edits to simplify your workflow while checking the footage, export and final upload that determine what viewers actually see.

sections.heading: Why it helps
paragraphs: Edits brings phone editing and direct Instagram or Facebook sharing into one workflow, with exports that have no added watermark. That convenience can save steps. It does not mean a video looks bad simply because you used another editor. Instagram also creates encoded playback versions after upload.

sections.heading: Try this
paragraphs: Check the video at each handoff so you know where a problem first appears.
bullets: Start with the original camera clip. Check focus, lighting and motion before adding effects. A larger export setting cannot recreate missing detail in a soft source.

Build a short vertical edit with readable captions and room around important text. Review the export resolution and frame rate, then save a clean master instead of repeatedly downloading and reuploading copies.

Watch that saved file before posting. After upload processing, compare it with playback on Instagram. If only the posted version looks different, investigate upload and playback settings before changing your whole editing setup.

title: CapCut: check the export before you post
excerpt: Choose export settings for your footage and destination, then inspect the saved file instead of trusting a resolution label alone.

sections.heading: Why it helps
paragraphs: A sharp edit can still leave CapCut with the wrong crop, soft detail or awkward motion. The export panel gives you control over resolution, frame rate and bitrate. Those settings work together. Selecting 4K alone does not guarantee a better result on Instagram or any other platform.

sections.heading: Try this
paragraphs: Make a short test export before rendering a long project.
bullets: Set the canvas for the destination. For a full screen vertical social clip, a 9:16 layout is a useful starting point. Check faces, captions and logos inside that frame rather than stretching a horizontal image.

Open Export and check resolution, frame rate and bitrate together. Use settings your source and intended platform support. Higher bitrate can preserve more detail, but it also increases file size; maximum settings are not automatically the right delivery choice.
Play the actual exported file with sound. Inspect movement, small text and dark areas. Compare it with your source, then upload the clean master and review the posted result after processing.

sections.heading: Your next move

paragraphs: Build a small test scene first, especially when your script includes names or specialist words.

title: Make your next cover art work before anyone presses play.
excerpt: Your artwork needs to look good as a tiny thumbnail and arrive in the right format. Here is a clear checklist for your next single.

sections.heading: Give the song one visual idea
paragraphs: Choose a mood and a clear focal point before adding fonts or effects. Send the exact artist name, release title, references and distributor submission deadline. Supply original images you have permission to use, rather than screenshots.
Check the design both full size and as a small thumbnail. Look for readable text, sharp source images and important details too close to the edges.

sections.heading: Check the delivery file
paragraphs: DistroKid calls for JPG artwork in RGB color space. It recommends a square 3000 by 3000 pixel image, with a minimum of 1000 by 1000. Enlarging a small image cannot restore detail that was never there.

Its guidance excludes URLs, QR codes, prices, streaming service logos and social platform logos. It also warns against poor quality imagery and duplicate artwork across releases. Recheck your actual distributor’s requirements before submission; a design is not a guarantee of acceptance.

sections.heading: Build the release around it
paragraphs: Use the approved cover’s colors and visual idea to connect your social posts, reels and video direction. Each format still needs its own composition.
